extracted.intended_audience: founders, researchers and communications staff of new or small think tanks
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for designing and running communications for think tanks: identifying audiences, choosing channels and tools, building teams and partnerships, producing outputs, and monitoring impact to influence policy debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify main audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Think tanks need an audience to fulfil their missions. Identify your main audience and who will be interested in what you have to say, including the policy debates you aim to contribute to and the policy level you wish to influence (national, local, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by identifying who is interested in the issues your think tank is working on; who you are aiming to influence and who can support you (e.g. media, funders, NGOs, opinion makers). Remember audiences are not only policymakers, civil society and the media — other thinktankers and donors also play a role. Use stakeholder-mapping tools but don't get overly focused on exhaustive mapping at the beginning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link audience identification to research uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of who will listen is relevant to your research uptake strategy: involve or consider various audiences throughout the whole process so research is relevant to their needs and interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan engagement with audiences across the research lifecycle to ensure relevance; consult 'research uptake' resources for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask audiences directly about preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach your audiences and ask them how they prefer to access new ideas, how think tanks could communicate better, and for examples of good and bad experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use their answers to plan engagement. Example: a journalist highlighted 'accessibility and credibility of the sources' as very important — when a source works well, it is likely to be used again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice audience development (relationship-focused)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience development is about developing communications with existing and new audiences, not just increasing numbers; it focuses on understanding and building relationships to communicate relevant, timely, simple messages of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By understanding audiences you build trust and credibility so they seek your help and avoid communicating with audiences who are not interested in your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate objectives across audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all audiences need to be convinced to act on recommendations; some need convincing to support ideas, others need support developing and communicating their own arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor messaging and engagement levels depending on whether the goal is action, endorsement, capacity building, or joint advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stakeholder mapping tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a selection of tools for analysing and mapping stakeholders (e.g., GIZ Youth development stakeholder analysis; Net-map toolbox; IIED stakeholder power analysis; ODI planning tools).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools can help analyse influence, power and relationships. The page lists several resources as starting points for stakeholder/power analysis and mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble the right team composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for a small team of 3–4 people including: an insider with deep policy/context knowledge; someone with facilitation skills and networks to engage policymakers; someone with technical skills; and a team leader who coordinates technical and political dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure roles cover political/contextual expertise, facilitation/networking, technical competence, and coordination. Size may be constrained, but include communications from the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage prior connections and shared experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the most of prior contacts and shared experiences to foster strong relationships and accelerate engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared history and expectations that ‘something good’ will happen help build trust more quickly than starting cold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base the team close to the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The delivery team should be as rooted close to the ‘action’ as possible and be made up of national staff; foreign staff must be immersed in the context for long periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proximity and local staff increase credibility and ability to build relationships; plan for immersion for non-local members to build effective connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish good team working practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Team members should communicate regularly and feel comfortable talking and listening in equal measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular internal communication and an inclusive culture improve delivery and stakeholder engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with high-capacity institutions for short-term change
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterparts with higher capacity are more likely to use your support for short-term change; lower-capacity institutions require a longer-term approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not mean avoiding low-capacity partners, but planning appropriate timelines and resources if capacity development is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate the role with government counterparts
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide with partners how much emphasis on getting results vs capacity development; for a results approach you may take a hands-on role, for capacity building a more reflective/limited-input approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify expectations and roles early to avoid mismatches in approach and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen but don't meet all counterpart demands
rubrics_metrics.description: While counterparts have deep local knowledge, maintain the value you bring; have discussions that consider different perspectives and view each other as partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance responsiveness to partner needs with providing independent analysis, methods, and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with existing in-country initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and coordinate with other teams or initiatives supporting policymakers to use evidence; seek complementarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid duplication and look for synergies; collaboration can strengthen uptake and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider setting up an advisory/steering group
rubrics_metrics.description: A steering group can help ensure work is relevant beyond immediate actors and pressure counterparts for rigorous engagement; approach institutions with cross-government mandates or representatives of other policy support initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use advisory bodies to broaden accountability and relevance; choose members who add legitimacy and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalise relationships (MoUs and agreements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider revising memoranda of understanding underpinning agreements to address issues like confidentiality or intellectual property clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal agreements clarify expectations, roles, data/IP handling and can prevent misunderstandings during partnerships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use partnership toolkits to structure agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply structured partnership toolkits (e.g., NESTA Partnership toolkit, The partnership toolbox) to identify the type of partnership needed and required agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toolkits guide choosing partnership types and drafting necessary clauses; use structured approaches rather than informal arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start communications early and assign responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Do communications from the start; define who will be in charge and what resources they will have — even if capacity is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a one-person communications function is better than none. Get researchers involved, and plan for capacity-building if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define success and desired impact at project start
rubrics_metrics.description: At the start of any project, think about what you are trying to achieve and what success looks like to choose the correct output for maximum impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defining objectives early guides channel and output choices; success metrics inform monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know how your audience consumes information
rubrics_metrics.description: If you know your audience, you know how they consume information; audiences may prefer blogs, videos, briefings, virtual conferences, social media, press releases, infographics or one-to-one meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure, speak with stakeholders or intermediaries to identify preferred channels; choose outputs accordingly to maximize engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be realistic about communications budgets but be creative
rubrics_metrics.description: Be realistic about what you can afford but don't assume expensive-looking tools are unaffordable; low-budget videos and simple outputs can still be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do the best with available resources; a low-budget product can look low-budget and still be impactful; avoid foregoing effective formats solely due to perceived cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use events strategically and cost-effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Events can be cost-effective content producers: search for free venues, co-organise, keep events simple, brief speakers, allow time for engagement and networking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit refreshments if funds are tight (context-dependent), record or livestream events, live-tweet, upload presentations, write follow-up content, interview panelists, and add attendees to databases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use events to generate multi-format content
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is an opportunity to produce new content across formats (recordings, blogposts, videos, tweets, presentations) and to expand your contact base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan in advance to capture content and repurpose it across channels to extend reach and longevity of messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose tools and channels appropriate to project and organisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each think tank must choose the mix that works best for each project and for the organisation; ensure synergy between organisational focus/themes and project outputs/audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger organisations may need project-based mixes due to broader themes; check for alignment between organisation-level and project-level tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess tools using guiding questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing tools/channels consider: resources (funds and people), whether tools reach main audiences, balance between content and outreach, how to keep ideas on the public agenda, and whether tools are linked/support each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical checklist: Do you have media skills? Reliable internet? Printing resources? Are any audiences not being reached? Is there sufficient original material? Are the tools deployed in an integrated way?

rubrics_metrics.name: Orchestrate communications for sustained presence ('communications as an orchestra')
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to introduce ideas and keep them on the public agenda as long as possible by producing excellent outputs that can be combined into sustained engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep journalists coming back, keep policymakers engaged across cycles, and retain researchers in debates; avoid one-off engagements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move beyond the classic single-report dissemination model
rubrics_metrics.description: The classic model (rigorous 40-page report + comms officer promoting it via launch event, press release, tweets) is no longer sufficient; develop multi-medium products to be accessible and competitive online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn research into multi-format, accessible products for diverse audiences rather than relying on invite-only events or PDF uploads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a communications health check
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate key areas — audiences, channels, messaging, systems, strategy, capacity and monitoring — to refine and improve communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer simple questions to pinpoint priorities; recognise communications involve strategy, tactics and resources, not only outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in communications capacity regardless of size
rubrics_metrics.description: Even very lean organisations should prioritise communications from the start; researchers will need to wear multiple hats (researcher, communicator, manager, leader) and may require capacity-building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for training and support; define who is responsible for communications and what resources they will have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a strong think tank brand
rubrics_metrics.description: Branding is more than a logo: it helps the organisation become what it aspires to be, own intellectual/cultural territory, and produce the right kinds of communications for the right audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start branding with a clear understanding of audiences and messaging; use brand to align organisational strategy and communications outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use non-linear, engaging research outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Move beyond PDFs and linear narratives; consider interactive websites (choose-your-own-adventure approaches), data visualisations and other engaging technologies to communicate research findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design outputs that allow different entry points and that surface lost links and materials that linear PDFs hide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be clear about what to monitor and why (MEL for communications)
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing a monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL) strategy for communications: be fully clear about what you are going to measure and why; pick a couple of indicators and use simple tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a regular (e.g., quarterly) learning meeting to present trends visually, brainstorm ideas, and fix issues. Ensure collected data is analysed and lessons are put to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with simple, practical indicators and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t do anything too fancy to begin with; choose a few useful indicators and simple tracking tools appropriate to new/small think tanks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most useful initial indicators vary by context; focus on a few that inform strategy and are feasible to track.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold regular learning meetings to use monitoring data
rubrics_metrics.description: Have periodic meetings to focus on learning and future strategy, using data visualisations to show trends and inform brainstorming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use meetings to convert monitoring into actionable changes and to iterate communications plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existing toolkits and frameworks for MEL
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Communications monitoring, evaluating and learning toolkits (e.g., ODI internal guidance) that provide frameworks, questions, indicators and tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toolkits can help ensure communications are strategic and that lessons are learned from what works and what doesn't.
